issues.legal_issue: The power to make a pre-emptive purchase of an immovable property is not an unfettered discretion when confined to significant undervaluation connected to tax evasion.
material_facts: The statutory scheme was introduced to counter tax evasion through understatement of the value of immovable property.

Government instructions and affidavits stated that the power was intended to be used where the apparent consideration was significantly below fair market value, generally by 15% or more, and with a reasonable margin for estimation error.
The authority was required to record written reasons, and the affected parties could rebut an inference of attempted tax evasion by showing bona fide reasons for the agreed price.
issues.conclusion: The power, construed as applicable only in cases of significant undervaluation connected to an attempt to evade tax, did not confer arbitrary or unfettered discretion and was not invalid under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Chapter XX-C of the Income Tax Act, 1961, must be construed in light of its purpose of countering tax evasion; significant undervaluation may support a rebuttable presumption of that purpose, but the purchase order must rest on written reasons germane to the statutory object. The Court relied on K.P. Varghese v. Income-Tax Officer, Ernakulam, which rejected a literal construction that would capture bona fide transactions, and referred to Commissioner of Income-tax, Gujarat-II v. Smt. Vimlaben Bhagwandas Patel and Anr. in considering the inference arising from substantial undervaluation. Article 14 was not violated on this confined construction.

rule.if: statutory_preemptive_purchase_scheme and significant_undervaluation and tax_evasion_object and rebuttable_evasion_inference and written_relevant_reasons

predicates.statutory_preemptive_purchase_scheme: The proceeding concerns a statutory scheme allowing the government to purchase property that parties have agreed to transfer.
predicates.significant_undervaluation: The agreed consideration is significantly below the property's fair market value, allowing for a reasonable margin of estimation error.
predicates.tax_evasion_object: The scheme is directed at countering tax evasion through understatement of property value.
predicates.rebuttable_evasion_inference: The authority may infer an attempt to evade tax from significant undervaluation, while the parties may offer evidence to rebut that inference.
predicates.written_relevant_reasons: The authority records reasons that are connected to the scheme's purpose.

issues.definition: When a statutory pre-emptive purchase scheme targets tax evasion, significant undervaluation can support a rebuttable inference of evasion, and a purchase power exercised for relevant written reasons is not arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: A reasonable opportunity to show cause must be given to the intended parties before an adverse pre-emptive purchase order is made.
material_facts: The statutory chapter contained no express provision requiring a hearing before a purchase order.
A purchase order had serious civil consequences and could imply that the parties had attempted tax evasion.
Significant undervaluation could result from bona fide circumstances, including urgency, disputed title, or an existing lease, and the parties needed an opportunity to explain those circumstances.
The statutory decision period was short, but the resulting inquiry could be summary rather than omitted altogether.
issues.conclusion: The requirement of a reasonable opportunity to show cause must be read into the statutory scheme, particularly for the intended seller and intended purchaser.
issues.legal_principle: Principles of natural justice supplement valid legislation unless expressly or by necessary implication excluded. A reasonable hearing is ordinarily required before action with adverse civil consequences, and urgency does not exclude it unless the circumstances warrant that departure. The Court relied on Union of India v. Col. J.N. Sinha and Anr., including its reference to A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India, and Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation. The requirement was also necessary to preserve compliance with Article 14.

rule.if: preemptive_purchase_proceeding and affected_parties_face_adverse_civil_consequences and parties_can_offer_bona_fide_explanation and no_express_hearing_exclusion

predicates.preemptive_purchase_proceeding: The authority is considering a government purchase of property already agreed to be transferred.
predicates.affected_parties_face_adverse_civil_cons: The proposed order would adversely affect the intended parties and carry an implication of attempted tax evasion.
predicates.parties_can_offer_bona_fide_explanation: The parties may have genuine reasons for agreeing to a price below estimated market value.
predicates.no_express_hearing_exclusion: The governing scheme does not expressly exclude a hearing or make one impossible by necessary implication.

issues.definition: When a proposed pre-emptive purchase has adverse consequences and the parties can explain the transaction, they must receive a reasonable chance to show cause unless the governing scheme excludes it.

issues.legal_issue: Written reasons supporting a purchase order must be communicated to the affected parties with the order.
material_facts: The statutory scheme required the authority to record its reasons in writing and to serve a copy of its order on specified affected persons.
The reasons for the challenged order were neither stated in the order nor communicated to the affected parties.
Communication of reasons enables an aggrieved party to challenge erroneous, irrational, or irrelevant reasoning and deters arbitrary action.
issues.conclusion: The reasons for a purchase order must be communicated to the affected party, either within the order or separately with it.
issues.legal_principle: A requirement to record reasons is not satisfied, for the purposes of an effective challenge, by reasons kept undisclosed. Where the governing scheme requires written reasons and service of the order, the served order must include the reasons or be accompanied by them. Communication both enables judicial review and restrains arbitrary decision-making.

rule.if: preemptive_purchase_order and written_reasons_required and affected_party_receives_order and reasons_not_communicated

predicates.preemptive_purchase_order: An authority makes an order for the government to purchase property subject to an agreement to transfer.
predicates.written_reasons_required: The governing scheme requires the authority to record reasons for the order in writing.
predicates.affected_party_receives_order: The governing scheme requires or provides for the order to be served on an affected party.
predicates.reasons_not_communicated: The affected party does not receive the reasons with the order.

issues.definition: When a written-reasons purchase order is served on an affected party, the reasons must be communicated with that order.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-emptive purchase cannot extinguish bona fide leasehold or possessory encumbrance rights unrelated to the transaction's tax evasion where the agreed sale is subject to those rights.
material_facts: A purchase order caused the property to vest in the government free from all encumbrances and required persons in possession to surrender it.
A bona fide lessee or encumbrance holder could have rights unrelated to any undervaluation or tax evasion by the parties to the proposed sale.
Where a property was agreed to be sold subject to existing rights, the stated consideration could reflect the reduced value of the burdened property rather than the value of an unencumbered property.
Where the agreement instead provided for a sale free of encumbrances or leasehold interests, the apparent consideration could include the value of those interests.
issues.conclusion: The words providing for vesting free from all encumbrances were invalid under Article 14; the possession-delivery provision must be read down so that it does not apply to bona fide lessees or bona fide possessory encumbrance holders when the sale is subject to their rights. Where the agreed sale is free of those rights, affected holders may claim their fair value from the purchase price paid to the owner.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits extinguishing bona fide third-party rights without a rational connection to the anti-evasion purpose, particularly where the agreed consideration reflects the property subject to those rights. The Court considered sections 269UE(1), 269UE(2), 269UE(5), and 269UA(e) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. A bogus lease or encumbrance may be treated as legally ineffective; the Court did not extend protection to such sham interests.

rule.if: preemptive_purchase_proceeding and bona_fide_third_party_property_right and sale_subject_to_that_right and right_holder_unconnected_to_evasion

predicates.preemptive_purchase_proceeding: The government seeks to purchase property that parties have agreed to transfer.
predicates.bona_fide_third_party_property_right: A third party holds a genuine leasehold or possessory encumbrance right in the property.
predicates.sale_subject_to_that_right: The agreed transfer is subject to the third party's right rather than requiring the property to be delivered free of it.
predicates.right_holder_unconnected_to_evasion: The third-party right holder is not involved in the attempted tax evasion alleged in the transaction.

issues.definition: A genuine third-party property right survives a government purchase when the agreed sale is subject to that right and its holder is unconnected to the alleged evasion.

issues.legal_issue: A monthly tenancy may continue after a pre-emptive purchase if the sale agreement does not require vacant possession, but the tenant does not retain rent-control protection against the government as owner.
material_facts: The Court treated monthly tenants as lessees, although their rights were limited.
If the agreement did not require vacant possession or termination of the tenancy, the tenancy continued after the purchase order.
The rent-protection laws did not apply to property owned by the Central Government, so the government could terminate the tenancy.
The Court held that loss of rent-control protection did not give rise to compensation.
issues.conclusion: A monthly tenancy continues if the agreement does not provide for vacant possession or its termination, but the tenant loses the protection of rent-control laws after the government purchase and is not entitled to compensation for that loss.
issues.legal_principle: A monthly tenant is a lessee in law, and the effect of a purchase on the tenancy depends on whether the agreed sale provides for vacant possession or termination. The Court distinguished continuation of the tenancy from statutory rent-control protection, which did not apply to government-owned property, and held that the loss of that protection was not a compensable interest.

predicates.preemptive_purchase_proceeding: The government purchases property that parties have agreed to transfer.
predicates.monthly_tenancy: A monthly tenant occupies the property under a tenancy.
predicates.sale_agreement_does_not_require_vacant_p: The agreement does not require the property to be transferred with vacant possession or the tenancy to be ended.

issues.definition: A monthly tenancy continues after purchase when vacant possession is not required, but it does so without rent-control protection against the government.

issues.legal_issue: A purchase order made without a reasonable opportunity to show cause and without communicating its reasons is invalid.
material_facts: The purchase order was made without a show-cause notice or an opportunity for the affected parties to respond.
The order did not state the reasons for purchase, and no reasons were communicated with it.
The Court had held that both a reasonable opportunity to show cause and communication of reasons were required.
issues.conclusion: The challenged purchase order was bad in law and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: A purchase order must comply with the implied hearing requirement and the duty to communicate its written reasons. Non-compliance with these requirements renders the order invalid. The Court applied its interpretation of Chapter XX-C consistently with Article 14 and the principles of natural justice.

predicates.preemptive_purchase_order: An authority makes an order for the government to purchase property subject to an agreement to transfer.
predicates.no_show_cause_opportunity: The affected parties are not given a reasonable chance to respond before the order is made.
predicates.reasons_not_communicated: The authority does not communicate the reasons for the order to the affected parties.

issues.definition: A pre-emptive purchase order is invalid when affected parties receive no reasonable opportunity to respond and the reasons are not communicated.

issues.legal_issue: An invalid purchase order may be reconsidered after a hearing, while completed purchases accepted without protest and purchases by third parties at public auction remain undisturbed.
material_facts: The challenged order had to be set aside, but the statutory scheme pursued the public purpose of countering tax evasion in property transactions.
Applying the original statutory time limit would have prevented the authority from reconsidering the transaction.
The Court directed that the filed statement be treated as resubmitted for reconsideration and permitted a fresh show-cause process and, if appropriate, a summary inquiry.
Some purchases had been completed, possession taken, and compensation accepted without protest; other properties had been bought by third parties at public auction.
issues.conclusion: The authority could reconsider the transaction after giving the affected parties a reasonable opportunity to show cause, with any inquiry being potentially summary. Completed purchases accepted without protest and purchases by third parties at public auction were not invalidated by the judgment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court limited the retrospective effect of its ruling to avoid defeating the statutory purpose while protecting the affected parties through a fresh hearing. It relied on India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu, where invalidation of a provision did not require repayment of amounts already collected, and preserved completed transactions and third-party auction purchases.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_preemptive_purchase_order and original_order_invalid and transaction_not_completed_and_accepted_without_protest and not third_party_public_auction_purchase

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_preemptive_p: The proceeding challenges an order for the government to purchase property subject to an agreement to transfer.
predicates.original_order_invalid: The original order is invalid because required procedural safeguards were not followed.
predicates.transaction_not_completed_and_accepted_w: The purchase has not been completed through possession being taken and compensation being accepted without protest.
predicates.third_party_public_auction_purchase: A third party has purchased the property at a public auction following the original order.

issues.definition: An invalid purchase order may be reconsidered after a reasonable hearing if the purchase has not been completed and accepted without protest and no third-party auction purchase has occurred.

issues.legal_issue: When a purchase order is made after reconsideration following the delayed setting aside of the original order, the government must pay interest on the apparent consideration to compensate for the delay.
material_facts: The original purchase order was set aside, but the Court allowed the authority to reconsider the transaction after a fresh hearing.
A later purchase order could cause the seller to receive the purchase amount years later than under the original order.
The seller had retained possession of the property during the intervening period, and the Court considered that fact and the rise in urban property values.
issues.conclusion: If the authority made a purchase order after reconsideration, the government was required to pay the seller the apparent consideration together with interest at 9 per cent per annum from the date of the original order.
issues.legal_principle: The Court fashioned monetary relief to address the delay caused by setting aside the procedurally defective order, while taking account of the seller's retained possession and the increase in property values. The interest direction formed part of the Court's case-specific remedial order.

predicates.preemptive_purchase_order_set_aside: A court sets aside an original order for the government to purchase property.
predicates.authority_later_makes_purchase_order: The authority makes a new purchase order after reconsideration.
predicates.seller_receives_consideration_late: The seller receives the purchase consideration later because the original order was set aside and the matter reconsidered.

issues.definition: When a purchase order is set aside and a later order delays payment to the seller, the seller receives interest to compensate for that delay.
